findings.title: queue.Queue.shutdown() does not exist before Python 3.13
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches `queue.ShutDown`. Both `Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were only added in Python 3.13 (PEP 578 / bpo-... added in 3.13). Sentry currently targets Python 3.11/3.12 in production, so this call will raise `AttributeError`/`AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'` at runtime. Because the call is wrapped in a bare `except Exception: logger.exception(...)`, the error is swallowed, but the net effect is that worker threads are never actually signaled to stop (they remain blocked in `work_queue.get()`), causing `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` to time out on every shutdown and the daemon threads to leak for the life of the process.

findings.title: Workers can block forever on shutdown since queue has no sentinel/unblock mechanism
findings.body: Since `queue.Queue.shutdown()` isn't available on the Python version in use (see above), there is no fallback mechanism (e.g. a sentinel value or `put_nowait`) to unblock worker threads doing a blocking `get()` on an empty queue. As a result, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` cannot reliably stop workers that are idle-waiting, leading to resource leaks (threads never terminate) and `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` effectively not fully cleaning up, which could keep stale state (open sentry_sdk transactions, DB connections, etc.) running after the strategy is supposedly closed.

findings.title: get_committable_offsets does an O(gap) linear scan every second
findings.body: `get_committable_offsets` iterates `range(start, max_offset + 1)` for every partition on every tick of the 1-second commit loop. If a message is delayed/stuck (e.g. a slow group) while many offsets pile up behind it, this becomes a large linear scan repeated every second, consuming CPU proportional to the gap size. Given the stated motivation of the PR is to avoid slow items blocking the pipeline, a slow item can still cause this scan to balloon, partially offsetting the perf benefit this PR intends to deliver.

findings.title: WorkItem retains full Message object unnecessarily, inflating queue memory
findings.body: `WorkItem` stores the entire original `message` (including the raw Kafka payload) even though only `partition`, `offset`, and the decoded `result` are ever used by `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. For a backlog of thousands of queued items (which this feature expects to build up when a group is slow), this needless retention of the raw message/payload bytes in every work item increases memory pressure substantially.

findings.title: max_workers=0 silently falls back to default num_queues
findings.body: `num_queues=max_workers or 20` treats `max_workers=0` the same as `None`, falling back to the default of 20 queues instead of raising an error or honoring an explicit (if nonsensical) value of 0. This could mask a configuration mistake silently.

findings.title: Queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash() for consistent routing
findings.body: `get_queue_for_group` uses the builtin `hash(group_key)` to pick a queue index. Python's string hashing is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED) by default, so while this is consistent for the lifetime of a single process (satisfying in-process ordering guarantees), it is non-deterministic across process restarts/rebalances. This isn't a functional bug given the stated invariants, but is worth calling out as fragile/surprising if used anywhere assuming cross-process determinism (e.g. tests asserting fixed indices, or future features relying on sticky partitioning across restarts).
